properties.name: The exhaustive check was BUILT and IS RUNNING over every skill — and it structurally cannot express a per-CLASS obligation, which is exactly why Artifact had a mechanic the others did not
properties.statement:
CHECKED 2026-08-28 against source, because Anthony asked whether the exhaustive check had actually been tried or only discussed: *"haven't we tried the exhaustive check already (I might be mistaken)?"*

**HE IS NOT MISTAKEN. IT EXISTS, IT IS IMPLEMENTED, AND IT RUNS OVER EVERY SKILL.** `HealCategory::ALL` with its exhaustive-match tests in `crates/reflow2-core/src/heal.rs`; dozens of `every_*` tests across the core test suite; and for skills specifically, `crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/served_skills.rs` iterates `SKILLS` three separate times while `tools/skill_lint.py` walks every skill directory.

═══ ⭐⭐ AND THAT IS WHY IT DID NOT CATCH THE ARTIFACT CASE ═══

**EVERY EXHAUSTIVE SKILL CHECK ASSERTS A UNIVERSAL PREDICATE.** Read from source: byte-identical to its kit source; has a non-empty description; appears in the served catalogue; states the graph-text-is-data rule; references only tools that exist; mirrors match across the three trees. Each is true-of-all-skills by construction.

**A flat loop over a flat set can only carry an obligation that applies to every member.** It has no vocabulary for *"this skill owes REPORTS mechanics and that one does not"*. So the exhaustive check did not fail — it succeeded completely, at its own scope, which is why the one universal mechanic sits at 23/23 while every other sits between 5 and 18.

═══ THE THREE TIERS, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS WHERE THE PAIN IS ═══

    UNIVERSAL obligation   → exhaustive loop            → WORKS. 23/23.
    PER-SKILL obligation   → 3 hand-written contracts   → N edits; the file itself
                                                          notes TWICE they are
                                                          "the same shape"
    PER-CLASS obligation   → NOTHING EXISTS             → Artifact's mechanic
                                                          never propagated

`ASK_CONTRACT`, `LINK_CONTRACT` and `OPTIMIZE_CONTRACT` are composition attempted by copy-paste: the right idea, expressed by duplication, bound to one skill each by its own loop.

═══ ⭐ THE MOSA ARGUMENT, WHICH IS ANTHONY'S AND IS SOUND ═══

*"I also feel like it fits the MOSA type concept better than exhaustive checks."* It does, and the reason is structural rather than aesthetic: a MOSA module is SEVERABLE and meets a stated INTERFACE, so it can be composed selectively, replaced, or upgraded without touching its neighbours. **An exhaustive check has neither property** — it is one monolithic predicate over the whole population, cannot be applied to a subset, and cannot be replaced for one member without weakening it for all. `dec:mosa-conformance` already asks whether reflow2 should report MOSA conformance given it computes most of the criteria; this is the same concept turned inward on reflow2's own skill surface.

═══ ON DEPENDENCY INJECTION IN RUST — IT IS ALREADY IN THIS CODEBASE ═══

*"potentially using dependency injection if that can be done in rust"*. It can, and it is not a new pattern here. **Rust has NO inheritance at all**, so composition via traits is the only idiom available — his stated preference is what the language forces. And the project already does constructor injection: `KvBackend` is a six-method trait with two implementations (`RocksBackend`, `MemoryBackend`) held as `Box<dyn KvBackend>` inside `StorageEngine`. The pattern he is describing for skills is the one already load-bearing under the store.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that composition is worth its cost here. It establishes only that the exhaustive check was genuinely tried, works at its scope, and cannot reach per-class obligations — so "just add an exhaustive check" is not an available answer to the Artifact case. The over-engineering counterweight on the parent node stands, and where the composition would LIVE (skill_lint, SKILL.md frontmatter, or the Rust build) is unchosen with materially different costs.
